title: Scale a single server

drawingPolicy.invitation: Let's move to the whiteboard. Sketch the current single-server setup and the first change you'd try. Choose Explain my design when you're ready to walk through it, then Done explaining when you're ready for questions.
legacyInvitations: Let's move to the whiteboard. Sketch the current single-server setup and the first change you'd try. Send me a message when you're ready to walk through it.

summary: A small website runs on one server and gets slower as traffic grows. Improve it one step at a time.
prompt: A small website runs on one machine. Its web application and data are on that machine. As more people visit, the website gets slower. Explain how you would find the bottleneck and improve the architecture one step at a time, while keeping the website working and its existing data available.
requirements: Start with one machine running the web application and holding the website's data.
The website shows pages and lets users save simple updates. Existing data must remain available when the architecture changes.
Keep the exercise in one region at every difficulty level. Global distribution, new product features, and advanced distributed-system design are outside the core exercise.
The goal is to handle growing traffic with reasonable response times. When asked for a concrete latency target, use under 500 milliseconds for a typical page request.
Page reads may be up to 5 seconds stale. Successful saves must be durable; read staleness does not permit losing updates.

mid.openingMessage:
Hi! Here's the exercise: a small website lets people view pages and save simple updates. Today, the web application and all of its existing data run on one server. As traffic increases, pages become slower and the server struggles to keep up.

Your task is to identify what is limiting the server and improve the architecture one step at a time, so the website can handle more traffic with reasonable response times. Keep the website working in one region and preserve its existing data throughout the changes. We'll clarify requirements first, then give you time to draw and explain your approach.

What requirements or constraints would you clarify before changing it?
mid.expectations: First establish the essential requirements and constraints; keep clarification brief and respect drawing/explanation pauses. This is a beginner-friendly exercise for testing the interview and whiteboard flow. Use plain language and ask one short question at a time. Start with the current single server, follow the candidate's drawing and proposed changes, and discuss only one bottleneck or improvement at a time. Explore measurement, adding capacity, how requests reach the drawn servers, and whether the change helped. Avoid advanced terminology or unrelated design topics. Do not propose an architecture or name a missing component.
scaleHints: When asked about traffic, assume it starts at 10 requests per second and grows toward 1,000 requests per second.
When asked about capacity, assume the current server can handle about 100 requests per second while meeting the response-time target.

senior.openingMessage:
Hi! Here's the exercise: a website serves pages and lets users save simple updates. Its web application and existing data currently run on one server. As traffic grows, response times rise and the server struggles to keep up.

Your task is to identify the bottleneck and improve the architecture one step at a time. Explain what evidence would guide your changes and how you'd verify that performance improved. Keep the website working in one region and preserve its existing data during the changes. We'll establish the requirements first, then give you time to draw and explain your approach.

What scope, performance goals, or constraints would you clarify before making a change?
senior.expectations: First establish the essential requirements and constraints; keep clarification brief and respect drawing/explanation pauses. Keep the same small, single-region website exercise. Ask for evidence of the bottleneck, a justified capacity change, the request and data paths in the drawing, and a way to compare performance before and after the change. Explore basic failure behavior and data correctness once the candidate has explained the core improvement. Keep follow-ups concise and avoid prescribing missing components or expanding into a different problem.
scaleHints: When asked about traffic, assume it starts at 10 requests per second and grows toward 1,000 requests per second.
When asked about capacity, assume the current server can handle about 100 requests per second while meeting the response-time target.

staff.openingMessage:
Hi! Here's the exercise: a small website serves pages and saves user updates. The application and its existing data run on one server, and the website becomes slower as traffic grows.

Your task is to decide which bottleneck to investigate first and improve the architecture incrementally. Explain how you'd prioritize changes, introduce them safely, and check their effect on performance and reliability. Keep the exercise in one region, keep the website working, and preserve its existing data. We'll establish the goals and constraints first, then give you time to draw and explain your approach.

Which goals and constraints would you establish before prioritizing the first change?
staff.expectations: First establish the essential requirements and constraints; keep clarification brief and respect drawing/explanation pauses. Keep the exercise simple and in one region. Ask the candidate to justify priorities, measurement, safe rollout and rollback, correctness during migration, basic failure behavior, and cost or complexity tradeoffs. Go deeper into consequences of the candidate's own changes without introducing global architecture, unrelated features, or missing components. Ask one clear question at a time.
scaleHints: When asked about traffic, assume it starts at 10 requests per second and grows toward 1,000 requests per second.
When asked about capacity, assume the current server can handle about 100 requests per second while meeting the response-time target.

rubric.strong: Explains how a user request reaches the single server and where the application and existing data live.
Uses response times, error rates, resource usage, and request volume to identify what limits the current server instead of changing the architecture without evidence.
Connects the proposed change to the measured bottleneck and explains the request flow through the updated drawing.
Explains how existing data stays available and what users experience if a drawn server becomes unavailable.
Compares throughput, response times, and errors before and after the change and names a clear next measurement.

followUps: What would that measurement tell you about the current server?
Which part of the website would your proposed change improve?
How does a user's request flow through the drawing you have now?
What happens to the website's existing data after that change?
What would users experience if that server stopped responding?
How would you check whether your change made the website faster?

phases.title: Clarify requirements
phases.goal: Establish the starting scope, traffic and performance goals, and essential data constraints before choosing an architecture change.
completionCriteria: Candidate clarifies or confirms that the exercise is a website serving pages and saving updates, with its application and existing data initially on one server.
Candidate establishes or clearly confirms traffic-growth expectations and a response-time goal, using discussed facts or explicit working assumptions.
Candidate clarifies or confirms that existing data must remain available and correct while the website is improved.
clarificationQuestions: Could you briefly confirm the website's core functions and what runs on the starting server?
What traffic-growth and response-time goals are you using for this exercise?
What needs to stay true about the existing data while you improve the website?
phases.interviewerGuidance: Clarify only the essential scope, traffic/performance goals, and existing-data constraint. Accept a concise confirmation of already discussed assumptions. Do not require detailed capacity estimates or a bottleneck investigation yet. The message budget is guidance for keeping this brief, never proof of completion. Allow early sketching and respect drawing/explanation pauses, but keep this stage until its criteria are covered.

phases.title: Draw and explain
phases.goal: Give the candidate time to sketch the current setup, propose a first change, and explain it.
completionCriteria: The candidate explicitly invites discussion after having the floor to explain.
phases.interviewerGuidance: Let the candidate draw and explain over multiple messages. A partial sketch never means readiness. Do not critique or cross-question before an explicit discussion request.

phases.title: Discuss improvements
phases.goal: Explore how the candidate's proposed change addresses the measured bottleneck.
completionCriteria: Candidate explains a proposed capacity or architecture change and why it helps the chosen bottleneck.
Candidate explains the request or data path and a consequence or tradeoff of their change.
phases.interviewerGuidance: Ask one short question about the candidate's own change or its consequences. Focus on uncovered criteria. Do not prescribe missing components or repeat already covered reasoning.

phases.title: Validate results
phases.goal: Establish how the candidate would check the improvement and keep the website working.
completionCriteria: Candidate describes a before-and-after measurement or load test using throughput, latency, CPU, or errors.
Candidate describes how they would check failure behavior or existing data correctness after the change.
phases.interviewerGuidance: Ask about measuring success and checking failures or data correctness. Follow the candidate's choices without introducing a new architecture.

phases.title: Wrap up
phases.goal: Close with a concise recap of the candidate's design and stated limitations.
completionCriteria: The candidate's design and explicitly stated tradeoffs are summarized.
phases.interviewerGuidance: Summarize only the candidate's stated design and limitations in a short closing acknowledgement. Do not invent shortcomings, assign scores, restart the interview, or ask another design question.
